title: Pig Kidney Patient Marks One Year Off Dialysis, a Transplant Milestone
excerpt: A 58-year-old New Hampshire woman has lived for one year with a kidney from a gene-edited pig — the longest any patient is known to have gone without dialysis after receiving a pig organ, Mass General Brigham and eGenesis announced Nov. 23.
content:
A 58-year-old New Hampshire woman has now lived for one year with a kidney from a gene-edited pig, the longest any patient is known to have done so — a milestone doctors say could point toward a future in which engineered animal organs ease the shortage of donor kidneys.

Molly Falco reached the milestone Sunday, Nov. 22, one year after she received the kidney on Nov. 22, 2025, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, eGenesis and Mass General Brigham announced Nov. 23. She is the first patient to surpass one year of dialysis independence after transplantation with a genetically engineered pig kidney.

Doctors say the organ filters waste from her blood, makes urine, and keeps her fluid and mineral levels in balance. Falco was born with a condition that damaged her kidneys and spent 11 months on dialysis before the transplant. She had complications soon after the surgery but has not needed a hospital stay since February. She has named the kidney Lily, after flowers relatives in Colorado sent after the surgery, and she has been cleared to travel there for Christmas.

“I’m amazed every day that it’s still working,” Falco told The New York Times. “I’m going to try to keep it as long as I can, and if it’s forever, that’s incredible.”

Her doctor, Dr. Leonardo Riella, who leads kidney transplant research at the hospital, cautioned that the milestone is not a finish line. “It is not a victory lap yet,” he told the Times. Pig organs remain experimental, and the kidney she received — eGenesis’ EGEN-2784 — came from a pig that had undergone 69 gene edits, including 59 to inactivate porcine retroviruses.

The result matters because more than a half-million Americans with kidney failure rely on dialysis, a treatment that cleans the blood when the kidneys cannot. Six patients have received eGenesis pig kidneys through the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Expanded Access pathway. The first died shortly after the transplant, of underlying heart disease. Two others had the kidneys for eight and nine months before their bodies rejected them. The other two patients who received pig kidneys this year still have them. A formal clinical trial of 33 patients at 10 medical centers across the country is set to begin in January.

Falco’s year beats the previous record of 271 days, set by another Mass General patient whose eGenesis kidney was removed in October 2025 after a decline in function. He later received a human kidney in January 2026.

Webb Watch 956 is reporting this as a medical research milestone. Pig kidney transplants are experimental and available only through controlled programs; they are not a treatment option a patient can request on their own.
